content: 1. The recommended dosage of mineral oil is 15-45 mL per day, taken orally, either as a single dose or divided doses. 2. For Kondremul, the recommended dosage is 30-75 mL per day, taken only at bedtime. It should not be taken with meals and can be administered as a single dose or divided doses. 3. Mineral oil reduces beta-carotene levels by binding to the drug in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Caution is advised, and monitoring is recommended. 4. Mineral oil decreases digoxin levels by inhibiting its absorption in the GI tract. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Caution and monitoring are advised. 5. Mineral oil reduces the levels of levonorgestrel, oral ethinyl estradiol, and ferrous bisglycinate by inhibiting their GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 6. Mineral oil decreases vitamin D levels or effects through mechanisms other than GI absorption. Caution and monitoring are advised. Concomitant use of mineral oil and vitamin D supplements should be avoided to prevent reduced vitamin D absorption. This interaction applies only to oral administration. 7. Mineral oil reduces antithrombin alfa levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 8. Mineral oil decreases antithrombin III levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 9. Mineral oil reduces argatroban levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 10. Mineral oil decreases bemiparin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 11. Mineral oil reduces bivalirudin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 12. Mineral oil decreases dabigatran levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 13. Mineral oil reduces dalteparin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 14. Docusate increases mineral oil levels by enhancing its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 15. Mineral oil decreases enoxaparin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 16. Mineral oil reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 17. Mineral oil decreases fondaparinux levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 18. Mineral oil reduces heparin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 19. Mineral oil decreases mestranol levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 20. Mineral oil reduces phenindione levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 21. Mineral oil decreases protamine levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 22. Mineral oil reduces sulfadiazine levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 23. Mineral oil decreases sulfamethoxazole levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 24. Mineral oil reduces sulfisoxazole levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 25. Mineral oil decreases vitamin A levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 26. Mineral oil reduces vitamin E levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 27. Mineral oil decreases vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 28. Lipid pneumonitis may occur if the patient is reclined during administration. 29. Mineral oil use may lead to fecal incontinence, intestinal malabsorption, impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, rectal discharge, anal pruritus, irritation, abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting. 30. Aspiration of mineral oil can result in lipid pneumonitis, particularly in children under 6 years, pregnant individuals, bedridden patients, or those with swallowing difficulties or conditions affecting swallowing or epiglottal function. 31. The risk of aspiration increases in elderly patients. 32. If taking other medications, mineral oil should be taken at least 2 hours before or after other drugs. 33. Consult a healthcare professional before use if experiencing abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. 34. Seek medical advice if there is a sudden change in bowel habits lasting more than 2 weeks. 35. Consult a healthcare professional if currently using a stool softener laxative. 36. Mineral oil should not be taken with meals. 37. Discontinue use and consult a healthcare professional if rectal bleeding occurs or if bowel movements do not occur after using the laxative, as this may indicate a serious condition. 38. If mineral oil is needed for more than one week, discontinue use and consult a healthcare professional. 39. It is unknown if mineral oil is excreted in breast milk; consult a healthcare professional before use. 40. Mineral oil is generally considered safe during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
